opus-5.5.text:
Well, the basic idea, which Eric Wefald and I worked on back in the late eighties, is that computation is itself an action. It takes time, and time has value, because the world doesn't wait while you think. So the question becomes: of all the computations I could do right now, which one is most likely to improve my eventual decision enough to be worth the time it costs?

You can frame that in decision-theoretic terms. Each computational step, say expanding a node in a search tree or running another simulation, has an expected value: the probability it changes which action you'd choose, times how much better that new choice would be. Then you subtract the cost of the time spent. If no computation has positive net value, you stop thinking and act. That gives you a principled answer to when to stop deliberating, which is something classical algorithms mostly just hard-code.

What falls out is quite intuitive. You shouldn't waste effort on moves that are clearly terrible, because more thinking won't change your mind about them. And you shouldn't agonize over two options that are nearly equal in value, because even if you pick the slightly worse one, you haven't lost much. The valuable computations are the ones where there's real uncertainty and real stakes: where a little more information might flip your decision and the flip actually matters.

Of course, computing the exact value of computation is itself intractable. You'd get an infinite regress if you insisted on doing it perfectly. So in practice you use myopic approximations: estimate the value of a single step as if it were the last one, and use simple learned or statistical models of how computations tend to change your estimates. Those approximations work surprisingly well. Some of the ideas show up, in a somewhat different form, in Monte Carlo tree search and bandit-based methods, where the allocation of simulations is essentially a metareasoning problem.

The broader point I'd make is that this is how we should think about bounded rationality. A real agent can't be perfectly rational, because perfect rationality would require infinite computation. What it can aim for is something like bounded optimality: being the best possible program for a given machine and environment. Metareasoning is one of the main ways to get there, because it lets the agent manage its own limited resources intelligently rather than following a fixed procedure regardless of the situation.

r001.rationale: It describes computation as an action and asks which computation to perform, giving examples such as expanding a search node or running a simulation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention alpha-beta pruning or describe it as a policy for selecting object-level computations.

r003.rationale: It says to choose computations likely to improve the eventual decision enough to justify their cost, and explains their expected value in terms of changing the choice and how much better it would be.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the starting point is to recognize that computation isn't free. Any real agent, biological or artificial, has limited time and limited hardware, and it has to act in a world that doesn't wait. So the question of what to think about is itself a decision problem, and I've argued for a long time, going back to work with Eric Wefald in the late eighties, that you should treat it as exactly that.

The basic idea is what we called rational metareasoning. A computation is worth doing if its expected value exceeds its cost. The cost is roughly the time it takes, which you can translate into the utility you lose by delaying action. The value of a computation is more subtle. A computation doesn't change the world directly. What it does is change the agent's beliefs about which action is best. So the value of computation is the expected improvement in the quality of the decision you eventually make, as a result of having done that computation. If you're already confident that action A is best, and a computation would only confirm that, it's worth nothing. If a computation might reveal that action B is actually better, then it has positive value, proportional to how much you'd gain by switching and how likely that switch is.

Now, computing that exactly is itself intractable, which is the obvious regress. In practice you use what we called the myopic approximation. You ask, if I did this one computation and then stopped and acted, what's the expected gain? That's a single-step estimate, and it's wrong in the sense that you often do more than one step, but it turns out to be a remarkably effective heuristic for selecting computations. In game-playing search, for instance, this gives you an algorithm that decides which leaf nodes to expand based on which ones could actually change the choice of move, rather than expanding everything to a uniform depth. And you get large improvements in play per unit of computation.

The deeper point is that this reframes a lot of what we call heuristics in AI. Alpha-beta pruning, iterative deepening, Monte Carlo tree search with its exploration bonuses, all of these can be understood as approximate solutions to the metalevel decision problem. They're ways of allocating a scarce resource, computation, towards where it's likely to matter. And I think once you see it that way, you also see that there's no such thing as a perfectly rational agent in the classical sense. What you can have is an agent whose program is the best program it could run given its limitations. I've called that bounded optimality. The design question becomes not "what's the right action" but "what's the right computation to do next in order to find a good action in the time you have." That shift, from object-level rationality to a rationality that accounts for the cost of thinking, is one of the more important conceptual moves in the field, and I think we still haven't fully worked through its implications.

r001.rationale: The response treats choosing which computations to perform as a decision problem and says a computation is worth doing when its expected value exceeds its cost, framing computations as selectable internal actions.

r002.rationale: It identifies alpha-beta pruning as an approximate solution to the metalevel decision problem and describes such methods as allocating computation toward where it is likely to matter.

r003.rationale: It defines computation value as the expected improvement in the quality of the eventual decision.

astra-6.text:
Well, the basic idea is to treat computation itself as an action. A computation has a cost—it takes time, and meanwhile the world may be changing—but it also has a potential benefit: it may enable you to make a better decision.

So at the meta-level, you're asking, “What is the expected improvement in the quality of my decision if I perform this computation?” You compare that improvement with the cost. You might examine another branch of a search tree, refine an estimate, or simply stop thinking and act. The point isn't to obtain the most accurate answer possible; it's to use your computational resources in whatever way produces the best outcome in the world.

Of course, there's a catch: deciding which computation to perform is itself a computational problem. If you insist on solving that optimally, you can get an infinite regress. So a practical agent needs relatively inexpensive ways of estimating the value of computation, often learned from experience. It should learn when further thinking is likely to change its decision enough to be worthwhile.

r001.rationale: It treats computation as an action and gives examples of selectable steps, such as examining a search branch or refining an estimate.

r002.rationale: It does not mention alpha-beta pruning or describe it as a policy for choosing object-level computations.

r003.rationale: It says to compare the expected improvement in decision quality from a computation with its cost.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the key idea is that computation is itself an action. It takes time, it uses resources, and we should choose it for the same reason we choose any other action: because we expect it to improve the outcome.

So, at the meta-level, the agent asks: if I do this computation—explore another branch of a search tree, for example—how might that change my decision, and how much better would that decision be? That expected improvement is the value of the computation. You compare it with the cost, including the cost of delaying action. Sometimes the right thing to do is think a little longer, and sometimes it’s to act now.

Of course, you don’t want to spend forever computing the value of computations. The meta-level has to be economical too. Typically, you learn approximate ways of recognizing which computations are useful. The goal isn’t to think as much as possible; it’s to use the available thinking time in the way that produces the best decisions.

r001.rationale: It describes computations as actions the agent chooses at the meta-level, including exploring another search branch.

r002.rationale: It does not mention alpha-beta pruning or describe it as a policy for selecting object-level computations.

r003.rationale: It says to choose a computation based on how much it is expected to improve the decision, weighed against its cost.
